summary: Specifies version 1.0 of Datagram Transport Layer Security, which brings TLS-style privacy to datagram protocols such as those running over UDP. It is based on TLS and aims to give equivalent security guarantees while preserving datagram semantics. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 6347.

plainLanguage.summary: DTLS is TLS for UDP. TLS assumes that everything sent arrives, in order, so it cannot run over a datagram transport. DTLS changes as little as possible to fix that: each record carries its own number, each handshake message carries a number and can be split across packets, and lost messages are sent again on a timer. It also adds a short cookie exchange so a server is not flooded by strangers.

subtitle: TLS rebuilt for datagrams, so UDP applications can be encrypted without giving up their delivery semantics.

tldr.problem: TLS assumes a reliable, ordered transport and breaks when records are lost or reordered, so applications built on UDP had no way to protect their traffic without writing a security protocol of their own.
tldr.mechanism: DTLS keeps TLS as it is and adds explicit sequence numbers and an epoch to each record, sequence numbers and fragmentation fields to each handshake message, a retransmission timer, and a stateless cookie exchange.
tldr.outcome: DTLS preserves datagram semantics, so a lost or reordered packet is still a lost packet. RFC 4347 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 6347.

today: RFC 4347 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 6347. It was also updated by RFC 5746 and RFC 7507.

sections.title: Why TLS Cannot Run Over Datagrams
sections.content:
TLS is the most widely deployed protocol for securing network traffic. Its main advantage is that it provides a transparent, connection-oriented channel, so an application protocol can be secured by putting TLS between the application layer and the transport layer. But TLS must run over a reliable transport channel, typically TCP, so it cannot secure unreliable datagram traffic.

Many application layer protocols now use UDP transport, in particular the Session Initiation Protocol and electronic gaming protocols. Designers of those applications were left with unsatisfactory choices: IPsec, which is suitable only for some applications; a custom application layer security protocol, which gives better end-to-end properties but takes a large amount of effort to design compared with running TLS; or nothing at all.

DTLS is the datagram-compatible variant of TLS. It is deliberately designed to be as similar to TLS as possible, both to minimize new security invention and to maximize the amount of code and infrastructure that can be reused. It runs in application space and needs no kernel modification, and it preserves the datagram property that data is not guaranteed to arrive or to arrive in order. The behaviour of media streaming, Internet telephony and online gaming is unchanged when DTLS is used, because DTLS does not compensate for lost or reordered traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS needs every byte to arrive, in order, which is exactly what UDP does not promise. Applications that want UDP were therefore left to write their own security protocol, which is a lot of work. DTLS is the answer: it keeps TLS as it is and changes only the parts that break when packets are lost.

sections.title: The Three Problems DTLS Fixes
sections.content:
The basic design philosophy of DTLS is to construct TLS over datagram, making only the minimal changes needed. Unreliability creates problems for TLS at two levels. In the traffic encryption layer, the record layer does not allow independent decryption of individual records: if record N is not received, record N+1 cannot be decrypted, because the cryptographic context is chained between records and the anti-replay and reordering protection uses a sequence number that is implicit in the records. In the handshake layer, the handshake is a lockstep exchange in which messages must be transmitted and received in a defined order, so it breaks when messages are lost.

The first fix is loss-insensitive messaging. The fix for both inter-record dependencies is the same and is well known from IPsec ESP: add explicit state to the records. DTLS adds an explicit sequence number, and it borrows the explicit CBC state that TLS 1.1 is adding to TLS records.

The second fix is reliability for the handshake. DTLS uses a simple retransmission timer to handle packet loss. Each handshake message is assigned a specific sequence number, so a receiver can tell at once whether a message is the one it expects next; if it is not, it queues the message until the earlier ones have arrived. Handshake messages may also be larger than a datagram, so each one carries a fragment offset and a fragment length and can be split across several records.

The third element is optional replay detection, using a bitmap window of received records as in IPsec. Records that are too old for the window, and records already received, are silently discarded. The feature is optional because a duplicated packet is not always malicious and can also result from a routing error.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things break when packets go missing. Records cannot be decrypted on their own, because each one depends on the last. And the handshake, which runs in fixed steps, stops if a step is lost. DTLS fixes the first by writing the sequence number into each record, and the second by numbering handshake messages and resending them on a timer.

sections.title: The DTLS Record
sections.content:
The DTLS record layer is almost identical to that of TLS 1.1. The only change is the inclusion of an explicit sequence number in the record, which lets the recipient verify the TLS message authentication code. The record carries a content type, the protocol version, an epoch, the sequence number, a length and the fragment.

DTLS 1.0 uses the version value 254, 255, which is the 1's complement of version 1.0. The maximal spacing between the TLS and DTLS version numbers makes records from the two protocols easy to tell apart. Future on-the-wire DTLS version numbers decrease in value while the true version number increases.

The epoch is a counter that is incremented on every cipher state change, and the sequence number identifies the record within that cipher state. As in TLS, the sequence number is set to zero after each ChangeCipherSpec message. When several handshakes run close together, the epoch lets a recipient tell apart records that share a sequence number but come from different cipher states. The epoch starts at zero and is incremented each time ChangeCipherSpec is sent. Implementations MUST NOT reuse the same epoch value within two times the TCP maximum segment lifetime.

Each DTLS record MUST fit within a single datagram, and several records may be placed in one datagram. Unlike IPsec, DTLS records carry no association identifiers, so the application must arrange to multiplex between associations, in the case of UDP by host and port number. The MAC is computed over the 64-bit value formed by concatenating the epoch and the sequence number in wire order. In DTLS, unlike TLS, a bad MAC does not have to end the connection: the receiver may simply discard the record and carry on.
sections.plainLanguage: A DTLS record is a TLS record with two extra fields at the front: a short epoch number and a longer sequence number. The epoch changes when the encryption keys change, so a receiver can tell two records apart even when they carry the same sequence number. Because records no longer depend on each other, a record that fails its check can be thrown away without ending the connection.

sections.title: The DTLS Handshake
sections.content:
DTLS uses all of the same handshake messages and flows as TLS, with three principal changes: a stateless cookie exchange to prevent denial of service attacks, modifications to the handshake header to handle message loss, reordering and fragmentation, and retransmission timers to handle message loss.

The cookie exchange guards against two attacks. An attacker can consume server resources by sending a series of handshake initiation requests, causing the server to allocate state and perform expensive cryptographic operations. An attacker can also use the server as an amplifier by sending connection initiation messages with a forged victim address, so that the server's next message, a Certificate message that can be quite large, floods the victim. The client sends a ClientHello, the server MAY answer with a HelloVerifyRequest containing a stateless cookie, and the client MUST retransmit its ClientHello with the cookie added. The server then proceeds only if the cookie is valid. The cookie length is 0 to 32 bytes, and the first ClientHello carries an empty cookie field. A server SHOULD perform a cookie exchange whenever a new handshake is performed. This mechanism does not defend against denial of service attacks mounted from valid IP addresses.

The handshake header gains three fields: a message sequence number, a fragment offset and a fragment length. The first message each side transmits in a handshake always has message_seq 0, each new message increments it, and a retransmission reuses the same value. A receiver keeps a next_receive_seq counter; a message below it MUST be discarded, and a message above it SHOULD be queued but MAY be discarded.

Handshake messages are divided into contiguous data ranges, each no larger than the maximum handshake fragment size, and each new piece is labelled with the offset and length of that piece while keeping the length field of the original message. A receiver MUST buffer fragments until it has the whole message, and MUST be able to handle overlapping fragment ranges, which lets a sender resend a message in smaller pieces during path MTU discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the real handshake starts, the server may ask the client to prove it can receive packets at the address it claims, by sending back a cookie. This stops someone hiding behind a false address from making the server do expensive work. Each handshake message then carries a number, so a receiver knows whether it is the next one it expects, and can put an out-of-order message aside until its turn comes.

sections.title: Timeout and Retransmission
sections.content:
DTLS groups handshake messages into flights, and each flight is viewed as a single unit for the purpose of timeout and retransmission. A client starts in the PREPARING state because it sends the first message; a server starts in the WAITING state with empty buffers and no retransmit timer.

In the PREPARING state the implementation does the work needed to prepare the next flight, buffers it and enters the SENDING state. In the SENDING state it transmits the buffered flight. If that was the last flight of the handshake it enters the FINISHED state; otherwise it sets a retransmit timer and enters the WAITING state.

There are three ways to leave the WAITING state. If the timer expires, the implementation retransmits the flight, resets the timer and returns to WAITING. If the implementation reads a retransmitted flight from the peer, it does the same, on the reasoning that a duplicate message usually means the peer's timer expired and part of the previous flight was lost. If the next flight arrives, the implementation moves to FINISHED when that was the last flight, or to PREPARING when it has a new flight to send. Partial reads cause no state transition and no timer reset. A server that wants a rehandshake moves from FINISHED to PREPARING to send a HelloRequest, and a client that receives a HelloRequest moves from FINISHED to PREPARING to send a ClientHello.

Implementations SHOULD use an initial timer value of 1 second, the minimum defined in RFC 2988, and double the value at each retransmission, up to no less than the RFC 2988 maximum of 60 seconds. The 1-second value is recommended instead of the 3-second RFC 2988 default to improve latency for time-sensitive applications.
sections.plainLanguage: The handshake runs in three steps on each side: get the next batch of messages ready, send them, then wait. While waiting, a timer runs; when it expires the batch is sent again. The timer starts at one second and doubles each time, up to sixty seconds, so that a busy link is not flooded by early retries.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
DTLS is a variant of TLS 1.1, so most of the security considerations are the same as those of TLS 1.1. The primary additional consideration is denial of service. DTLS includes a cookie exchange designed to protect against it. However, implementations that do not use this cookie exchange are still vulnerable, and DTLS servers that do not use it may be used as attack amplifiers even if they are not themselves experiencing denial of service. DTLS servers SHOULD use the cookie exchange unless there is good reason to believe that amplification is not a threat in their environment, and clients MUST be prepared to do a cookie exchange with every handshake.

The RFC also records that RC4 MUST NOT be used with DTLS, because the only stream cipher described in TLS 1.1 is RC4 and it cannot be randomly accessed. New TLS cipher suites MUST indicate whether they are suitable for DTLS usage and what adaptations, if any, must be made.
sections.plainLanguage: The security of DTLS is mostly the security of TLS. The one new worry is denial of service, because a server that answers anyone can be flooded, or used to flood someone else. That is what the cookie exchange is for, and the RFC says servers should use it and clients should always accept it.
